Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Troops in Jamaica captured an armed man Monday who had barged onto a Canadian airliner, robbed passengers and held six crew members hostage, Jamaica Information Minister Daryl Vaz said. A hostage-taker commandeered a CanJet flight at Sangster International Airport in Montego Bay, Jamaica. The crew members were not harmed, Vaz said. The hijacking suspect, described as a "mentally challenged" man in his 20s, had demanded that the Boeing 737 be flown to Cuba. The military captured him around 7 a.m. local time. The FBI helped Jamaican authorities handle the situation at the Jamaican government's request, a U.S. government source told CNN. The CanJet flight from Halifax, Canada, had made a scheduled landing at Sangster International Airport in the Jamaican resort city of Montego Bay and was scheduled to continue to Santa Clara, Cuba. Canadian Prime Minister Stephen Harper, who was in Jamaica, told reporters that he planned to travel to Montego Bay to meet with Jamaican Prime Minister Bruce Golding. Harper has been following the airplane security breach and may meet with the plane's crew later today. "The hijacking is that from a mentally challenged youngster and not anything that would be of concern in terms of an international incident," Vaz said. The suspect gained access to the plane Sunday night through the terminal in "a breach of security" that "will be investigated," Deputy Police Commissioner Owen Ellington told CNN. The gunman fired a shot in the boarding bridge as he entered, said CanJet Airlines Vice President Kent Woodside. No one was hit. CanJet Flight 918 was carrying 174 passengers and eight crew members, Woodside said. All the passengers were Canadian, he said. The suspect took an undisclosed number of passengers and crew members hostage before releasing all the passengers and two crew members, said Elizabeth Scotton, a spokeswoman for the company that manages the airport. Two of the six crew members who remained inside the plane Monday locked themselves in the cockpit, Vaz said. The suspect's father and Golding, who flew in by helicopter, were among those who negotiated with the gunman before his capture. The country's minister of national security also was at hand. The released passengers were taken to a hotel, and the airport was shut down for a time, Vaz said. The airport reopened shortly after the standoff, Woodside said. A CanJet airliner was on its way to Jamaica, he said, to take passengers on to Cuba or back to Canada. Christian Gosselin, a passenger on the flight, told his father that the gunman demanded cash from the plane's occupants. Vaz confirmed the account. "The guy wanted to have all their money," said Gosselin's father, Alphonse. "He [my son] told his girlfriend to take all the money and just take her passport and credit card and put it in her back pocket." Christian Gosselin was part of a 25-person wedding party headed to Cuba. He and his girlfriend were released by the hostage-taker, and they spoke to his father in New Brunswick, Canada, while waiting for another flight. "I didn't ask them too many questions; I was more concerned for their safety," the father said. "They were a bit shaken up. It was quite an experience." Another passenger, Brenda Grenier, called her husband and said the man apparently got aboard the plane as airport workers were loading bags. Grenier and her daughter were safe, her husband said by phone from his home in Nova Scotia, Canada. CNN's Joyce Joseph, Janet DiGiacomo, Jessica Jordan, Saeed Ahmed and Mike Brooks contributed to this report.

The ordeal began late Sunday night at Sangster International Airport around 10:30 p.m. local time. The Boeing 737-800, carrying 159 passengers and eight crew members, was preparing to depart for Halifax, Canada, with a scheduled stop in Santa Clara, Cuba.

According to police, Fray used fake identification to breach airport security before rushing the aircraft as passengers were boarding. Armed with a handgun, he forced his way past crew members and demanded to be flown to Cuba.

Initial moments on board were marked by chaos and panic as the gunman fired a shot into the air inside the cabin, passengers reported. 

Through swift negotiations led by Jamaican police and supported by the flight crew, officials persuaded the gunman to release all 159 passengers and two crew members in exchange for cash and personal belongings stolen from the hostages. The released passengers were escorted off the tarmac and taken to a nearby resort town hotel.

However, the gunman refused to surrender, holding the six remaining crew members hostage through the night as negotiators worked frantically on the tarmac.

### Tactical Entry at Dawn

Just before dawn, as negotiations stalled and the suspect grew increasingly erratic, members of the Jamaican Defence Force (JDF) counter-terrorism unit seized an opportunity to storm the aircraft.

Prime Minister Bruce Golding, who traveled to Montego Bay during the night to oversee the response, praised the calm composure of the flight crew and the swift execution by military forces.

"The crew members demonstrated incredible bravery and presence of mind," Golding said in a press conference. "And our security forces showed remarkable professionalism in bringing a potentially tragic situation to a peaceful resolution."

Information Minister Vaz noted that the suspect appeared to be "mentally disturbed" and was distraught over a failed personal relationship.

While Canadian and Jamaican leaders voiced relief over the safe resolution, the incident has raised severe questions about airport security at Sangster International Airport, one of the Caribbean's busiest tourist hubs.

Transport Canada announced Monday morning that it was sending a team of aviation security experts to Montego Bay to conduct a thorough review of how an armed individual was able to bypass security barriers and board a commercial airliner.

In Ottawa, Canadian Prime Minister Stephen Harper expressed deep gratitude to Jamaican authorities. 

"I spoke with Prime Minister Golding to express Canada’s appreciation for the swift and decisive action taken by Jamaican security forces," Harper said in a statement. "Our primary concern was the safety of the Canadians on board, and we are profoundly relieved that this ordeal has ended without loss of life."

CanJet, a Halifax-based charter airline, dispatched a replacement aircraft to Jamaica on Monday to transport the stranded passengers and crew back to Canada. 

Police say Fray faces multiple charges, including hijacking, illegal possession of a firearm, assault, and kidnapping.

The ordeal began shortly before 10:30 p.m. local time on Sunday when Fray, reportedly using fake credentials and forcing his way past security checkpoints, stormed the Boeing 737. Upon entering the cabin, he fired a shot into the air, demanding cash and asserting his core demand: immediate transport out of the country to Havana.

As dawn broke, Jamaican authorities determined that negotiations had stalled and authorized a tactical intervention. At approximately 6:40 a.m., members of the Jamaica Defence Force (JDF) Counter Terrorism and Special Operations Group, working alongside local police tactical units, executed a breach of the aircraft.

Military forces stormed the plane swiftly, taking the gunman completely by surprise. No shots were fired during the raid, and the suspect was tackled, disarmed, and taken into custody within minutes. None of the six remaining crew members sustained physical injuries during the extraction.

"The operation was executed with surgical precision," Jamaican Information Minister Daryl Vaz said in an official briefing following the raid. I am relieved to report that all hostages have been rescued safely, the perpetrator is in custody, and not a single life was lost."

"This appears to be the isolated act of a mentally disturbed young man," Vaz added, noting that a full-scale investigation had been launched to determine how the gunman managed to bypass multiple layers of airport security with a loaded firearm. For the more than 150 Canadian vacationers aboard Flight 918—many of them returning home from holidays in the resort town—the night was marked by panic, uncertainty, and incredible acts of calm from the flight crew.

**MONTEGO BAY, Jamaica (CNN) —** Jamaican special forces stormed a Canadian commercial airliner early Tuesday morning, successfully ending a harrowing eight-hour hostage crisis at Sangster International Airport that began when an armed man breached perimeter security and seized control of the Boeing 737, officials said.

"The threat has been neutralized, and all remaining crew members have been safely extracted," Jamaican Minister of National Security Horace Chang said during a brief press conference outside the airport's main terminal. "Our security forces executed a precise, decisive operation to ensure no innocent lives were lost."

### A breach on the tarmac

The crisis began at approximately 10:15 p.m. local time on Monday as Air Transat Flight 914 was undergoing final preparations for departure to Halifax, Nova Scotia. 

According to airport security footage and eyewitness accounts provided to CNN, the suspect used a stolen airport ground maintenance vehicle to crash through a secondary perimeter fence on the eastern boundary of the airport grounds. 

Armed with a handgun, the intruder drove directly onto the tarmac, ran up the boarding stairs, and forced his way past flight attendants into the aircraft's cabin. He fired a single shot into the ceiling of the plane to demand compliance, sending panic through the cabin, authorities said. No physical injuries were reported from the shot.

"We were settling in for the flight back home when suddenly there was screaming up front, and then a loud bang," passenger Brenda MacIntyre, a resident of Truro, Nova Scotia, told CNN via phone from the airport terminal. "A man rushed down the aisle shouting that nobody was leaving. Everyone was terrified, holding onto their kids."

### Tense negotiations and hostage release

Jamaican tactical units, alongside members of the Jamaica Defence Force (JDF), quickly surrounded the aircraft on a remote taxiway where the flight crew had managed to hold the plane.

During the initial hours of the standoff, trained police negotiators established communications with the suspect through the cockpit radio system and a mobile phone provided to him by ground crew. 

"The suspect was displaying erratic behavior and made demands including immediate refueling and clearance to fly to an undisclosed international destination," a senior Jamaican law enforcement official with direct knowledge of the situation told CNN, speaking on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss details publicly.

Negotiators persuaded the gunman to release all 174 passengers and two non-essential airline staff members roughly two hours into the ordeal in exchange for food and water. However, the suspect retained six crew members—including the captain and first officer—as leverage.

### The pre-dawn breach

As negotiations stalled shortly after 5:00 a.m. local time, and amid concerns over the suspect's escalating mental instability, the JDF's counter-terrorism unit authorized a dynamic entry.

Using specialized tactical ladders and flash-bang grenades, commandos simultaneously breached the front and rear doors of the aircraft. 

"We heard loud thuds, flash-bangs going off, and shouting from inside the plane," said CNN producer Patrick Fleming, who was near the perimeter line at the time of the raid. "Within minutes, officers were seen escorting the pilot and crew off the stairs, followed by the suspect in handcuffs."

The suspect, whose identity is being withheld pending formal charges, was transported to a high-security detention facility in Kingston. Authorities indicated he was known to local police but was not on any international counter-terrorism watchlists.

### Canada responds, security questioned

In Ottawa, Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau praised the swift resolution of the crisis and expressed relief for the safety of the crew and passengers.

Late in the evening of Sunday, April 19, 2009, an armed 21-year-old man bypassed security at Sangster International Airport in Montego Bay, Jamaica, and forced his way onto CanJet Flight 918.

Armed with a .38-caliber revolver, the gunman took everyone on board hostage, demanding to be flown to Cuba. What followed was a tense, nearly eight-hour standoff that ended in a swift, bloodless raid by Jamaican military commandos.
